title: Four women in the family tree (Matthew 1:1–17)
hookLine: a birthday photo with someone cropped out: why would Jesus' family tree keep the names a tidy one would cut?
tomorrow: Joseph's mind is made up. then he falls asleep…

lines: SOMEONE CROPPED OUT AT THE EDGE.
cards: A birthday post in the family group chat: an old photo, everyone squeezed onto one porch. Look closer, and someone at the edge has been cropped out. Families keep a tidy version of themselves, the one that gets framed.
This year reads one Gospel straight through, Matthew, from page one, and page one is a family tree. "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob." Father after father, the easy page to skim.
Then, four times before Mary, the pattern breaks, and in walks a name a tidy version would cut. So, one question for today: why keep them?

teach.b: Matthew opens: "The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham." A genealogy says who you are by saying whose you are.
"Judas begat Phares and Zara of Thamar": Tamar, a widow wronged by her father-in-law Judah, who in the end admits, "She hath been more righteous than I."
"Salmon begat Booz of Rachab": Rahab of Jericho, who hid two spies on her roof.

teach.h: TAMAR, RAHAB, RUTH, THE WIFE OF URIAS.
teach.b: "Booz begat Obed of Ruth": Ruth the Moabitess, a foreigner. And one woman Matthew never names: "her that had been the wife of Urias." That's Bathsheba, known here only by the husband King David sent to his death.
Matthew never says why these four. Some readers notice outsiders; some notice women wronged by powerful men; some notice women who acted when the men around them failed.
The answer the page gives either way: the line keeps the hard stories, by name.
Ruth is shared ground with a neighbor.

teach.h: THE LINE ENDS AT DAVID, OR GOES ON.
teach.b: Jewish tradition reads her book aloud at the festival of Shavuot, and it ends on a family line too, in the Jewish Publication Society's translation: "he is the father of Jesse, the father of David."
An old midrash on Ruth says the book was written to teach how great the reward is for acts of kindness.
Both traditions honor the foreign widow who chose to stay. And one honest difference: the Book of Ruth ends its line at David. Matthew carries it on to Jesus, whom Christians call the son of David.

how: Some churches read the genealogy from Matthew 1 aloud near Christmas, every name included, and some Christians read a Gospel straight through, a chapter at a time.

a list of a king's laws, in order

games.q: four women in the family tree — tap the pairs.

s: Matthew's family tree names only fathers
before Mary, it stops for Thamar, Rachab, Ruth and the wife of Urias.
Matthew calls Bathsheba by her name
he says "her that had been the wife of Urias."
the Book of Ruth ends with a family line that reaches David
"he is the father of Jesse, the father of David." Matthew carries the line on to Jesus.

games.q: your town is painting a mural of its history. some neighbors want only the founders on it; the people pushed out, and the newcomers, would complicate it. what does Matthew's first page model?
o: name them too: the outsiders and the wronged belong in the line.
keep to the founders: Matthew's list is about great men, really.
paint no names at all, so that nobody feels left out of it.
games.why: Matthew's line of fathers stops four times for Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and the wife of Urias: outsiders and wronged women, kept by name, with no explanation and no polish.

practice: Find a scrap of paper and write two names from your own family tree, by blood or by choice, that a tidy version would leave off: the outsider, the one who was wronged, the one with the complicated story.
Then rest with the paper in front of you. If you pray, you can hold those names before God; if not, let them simply be counted.

wordCard.voice: Genealogy. A family line, name after name. Matthew's opens his Gospel, and stops four times for women with hard stories.

orig.note: Greek: origin, birth. the word in Matthew 1:1 that the King James renders "generation."

carryVoice: Your line: every name counts. Even the one Matthew never said out loud. Year five, day one.
